stories.headline: Colorado Supreme Court rejects lawsuit seeking to stop Amendment 87 vote
stories.summary:
The Colorado Supreme Court on Friday rejected an attempt to nullify the vote on Amendment 87, allowing the proposal to raise taxes on the state's wealthiest residents to remain on the ballot. The lawsuit, filed by conservative activist Michael A. Hancock, argued on procedural grounds that backers used paid signature gatherers who did not follow state registration rules.

A Denver District Court judge ruled Oct. 21 that Hancock did not meet his burden of showing that any failure by petition gatherers violated laws meant to prevent misconduct. The Supreme Court affirmed that decision in a short, unsigned order and said a full opinion will be issued in due course. Some circulators had not completed state training, though they received training from the proponents.

Chris deGruy Kennedy, co-chair of the proponent group Protect Colorado's Future, said more than 130,000 voters who signed the petition deserve to have their signatures count. He acknowledged administrative oversights in registering some paid circulators. Hancock's attorney, Jason Dunn, called the result disappointing.

If passed, Amendment 87 would create a graduated income tax in which income above the first $500,000 is taxed at a higher rate than the current 4.4% flat tax. The proposal would cut taxes for most Coloradans.

stories.headline: Phil Weiser announces opposition to Amendment 87, Colorado's graduated income tax measure
stories.summary:
Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser, the Democratic nominee for governor, announced Friday evening that he opposes Amendment 87. The measure would raise taxes on people and businesses making more than about $500,000, raising an estimated $2 billion a year for health care, K-12 education and child care, while cutting taxes for those earning less.

Weiser said he supports a progressive income tax but considers this approach wrong for two reasons. He warned it could backfire if voters pass both Amendment 87 and Proposition 136, a conservative-backed measure capping income tax at 4.4%. If Proposition 136 received more votes, a court could theoretically block the tax increases while allowing the cuts, which Weiser said could reduce state revenue by $600 million. Supporters say the brackets are designed to take effect entirely or not at all. He also said the measure lacks a clear picture of how revenue would be spent.

Weiser joins Gov. Jared Polis, Sen. John Hickenlooper and Ken Salazar in opposition. Sen. Michael Bennet, Reps. Brittany Pettersen, Joe Neguse and Jason Crow, Treasurer Dave Young and the four Democrats on the Joint Budget Committee support the measure. It would replace the flat tax with six brackets.

stories.headline: Southern Colorado sheriff urges evacuations ahead of more flooding near Pagosa Springs
stories.summary:
The Archuleta County Sheriff's Office on Friday urged residents of low-lying areas to evacuate ahead of a weekend storm expected to bring heavy rain, snow and additional flooding. The county is still recovering from catastrophic floods that damaged more than 500 homes after the San Juan River in Pagosa Springs surged past 15 feet, its highest level in 115 years.

Roughly a quarter of county roads remain impassable. The National Weather Service issued a flood watch from late Saturday night through Monday morning for Pagosa Springs, Durango, Cortez and Silverton, with 1 to 3 inches of rain expected over saturated soils. The San Juan River is forecast to crest at 10.58 feet, just above minor flood stage.

A winter storm watch also covers parts of southwestern Colorado, with 8 to 15 inches possible in the mountains and gusts up to 55 mph. Officials warned storm conditions could delay first responders, and urged evacuees to bring documents, medications and supplies. Those needing help can call Archuleta County dispatch at 970-731-2160.

stories.headline: Avian flu detected at Weld County dairy, first Colorado dairy case in over two years
stories.summary:
Avian flu has been detected at a Weld County dairy, the first case at a Colorado dairy since August 2024. The USDA confirmed highly pathogenic avian influenza, and state health officials said the risk of humans becoming infected by drinking milk is low because pasteurization kills the virus.

The virus was found through routine bulk milk tank testing at Colorado State University's veterinary lab and confirmed by the National Veterinary Services Laboratory on Oct. 24. The unidentified dairy is under quarantine, so cows cannot leave and strict biosecurity protocols apply. Weekly testing will continue until the dairy tests negative two weeks in a row.

Colorado first found avian flu in dairies in April 2024, in an outbreak that grew to 64 dairies, and became the first state to mandate bulk milk testing. All herds were released from quarantine by December 2024. The state found the flu at a Weld County commercial chicken farm in January. In Washington state, the flu has spread to 27 dairy farms in the past three weeks.

stories.headline: Denver to face trial over arrest of man recording officers, judge says
stories.summary:
A jury will decide whether Denver has widespread practices that led officers to unconstitutionally arrest a man for recording and speaking to them, a federal judge ruled. U.S. District Chief Judge Regina Rodriguez advanced some claims by Zachary Manchas to trial in a Sept. 16 order.

Manchas was recording and yelling at two Denver officers during a high-risk traffic stop in Lower Downtown around 2 a.m. in June 2022. He was arrested for municipal interference, completed a deferred prosecution agreement, and the charge was dismissed. He sued the officers and the city over First Amendment and unlawful arrest claims.

Rodriguez initially concluded the officers were entitled to qualified immunity, but found the evidence sufficient for a jury to determine Denver has a widespread practice of arresting people who record officers. She wrote that Manchas's behavior was annoying and disrespectful, but that officers had already detained the driver and patted down the passenger before arresting him. Jurors could find he was unlawfully arrested, searched and retaliated against.

stories.headline: Jamal Murray scores 37 as Nuggets beat Suns in NBA Cup opener
stories.summary:
Jamal Murray scored 37 points on 10-of-18 shooting, including 7-of-9 from three, as the Nuggets opened NBA Cup play with a 127-120 win Friday night in Phoenix. Denver's next group stage game is Nov. 20 against the Rockets.

Christian Braun added a career-best 31 points and three steals, hitting six threes in the first half. Nikola Jokic had 18 points, seven rebounds and 10 assists. Cam Johnson returned after missing three games with an ankle injury, finishing with 12 points and 10 rebounds against his former team.

Phoenix's Dillon Brooks scored 20 first-half points before being ejected early in the third quarter for kicking Murray in the groin, according to the crew chief. Braun's late three-pointer gave Denver a 121-110 lead with 2:15 left. The Nuggets improved to 3-2 and completed a perfect two-game road trip. Alpha Diallo was listed as absent for personal reasons.

stories.headline: Broncos-Chiefs preview: Denver looks to contain Kenneth Walker in AFC West rematch
stories.summary:
The Broncos host the Chiefs at 2:25 p.m. Sunday at Empower Field at Mile High. If Denver wins, its odds of winning the AFC West jump to 49%, according to the New York Times simulator; a loss drops them to 14%.

In the season-opening 31-10 loss at Arrowhead, Denver missed 28 tackles, a 29.8% missed-tackle rate that was third-worst in an NFL game since 2018. Kenneth Walker rushed for 144 yards after contact and has 817 yards from scrimmage this season. Defensive coordinator Vance Joseph called the performance embarrassing and said the focus is preventing explosive plays.

Running back RJ Harvey is out with a knee injury, and rookie Jonah Coleman may start after leading the backfield in the second half of the win over Arizona. Denver has won three of the last four meetings with Kansas City.

stories.headline: Avalanche defenseman Josh Manson out about eight weeks with ankle injury
stories.summary:
Colorado Avalanche defenseman Josh Manson is expected to miss about eight weeks with an ankle injury, coach Jared Bednar said Friday. Manson was hurt during the opening period of a recent game.

The loss leaves a significant void on Colorado's blue line, as the veteran defender is a physical presence in the team's top pairings. The injury comes as the Avalanche have struggled with effort and consistency early in the season.

Colorado next faces the New Jersey Devils in the second and final meeting between the teams, looking to avenge an early-season loss.

stories.headline: Faster buses could come to more of Aurora as regional leaders study Colfax BRT extension
stories.summary:
The Denver Regional Council of Governments has completed a study of extending East Colfax bus rapid transit in Aurora from I-225 to E-470. The six-mile stretch is one of 12 high-priority corridors identified for long-term investment by 2050.

The study was led by DRCOG with help from Aurora, Adams and Arapahoe counties, RTD and CDOT. Planners estimate the project would cost between $52.9 million and $80.9 million and could raise daily ridership by about 25%. Side-running BRT lanes are one potential design.

DRCOG planner Cole Neder said congestion along the corridor could double by 2050 without action, given new housing and logistics development. There is no timeline or funding source yet. Business advocates noted that construction on the existing Colfax line has affected businesses, though open land farther east may reduce such impacts.

stories.headline: Data center fight heads back to Colorado Capitol
stories.summary:
Debate over data centers is expected to return to the state Capitol when legislators convene in January. In September, more than a hundred people protested a planned Colorado Springs data center known as Project Taurus, and the city council voted 7-2 to postpone a decision until April.

Aurora's council turned down a moratorium proposal, while Denver, Brighton and Littleton have implemented moratoriums. Douglas County approved about $19 million in tax incentives for a data center under construction in Parker. A divide is emerging between conservative jurisdictions embracing the facilities and progressive ones seeking to slow them, though Aurora's Republican mayor favors a moratorium.

Two data center proposals failed during the 2026 session. Supporters cite jobs, investment and tax revenue, while critics raise concerns about electricity costs, water use during drought and noise. Both sides say a framework is needed, but it is unclear whether agreement is possible by the end of the 2027 session.

stories.headline: Pikes Peak economy heads up after challenging years, officials say
stories.summary:
Colorado Springs Mayor Yemi Mobolade told the 30th annual UCCS Economic Forum that the city continues to attract residents, about six new ones a day, even as several major Colorado cities lost population. He cited Swire Coca-Cola's $475 million plant investment and 1,200 planned downtown apartment units.

The city was named best in the U.S. for small businesses by Bluevine, with Denver second, and visitors spent a record $3.1 billion in the Pikes Peak region last year. Mobolade said these are signs of progress rather than a victory lap.

The forum also addressed challenges after several years of fewer residential building permits, fewer home sales and slowing workforce growth. Chamber CEO Johnna Reeder Kleymeyer said Colorado is the sixth most regulated state, and officials said regulations weigh heavily on small businesses. Polis's Competitiveness Council recently reported that the state has lost its competitive edge.

stories.headline: Royal Gorge Bridge and Park could close briefly during operator transition
stories.summary:
The Royal Gorge Bridge and Park in Cañon City could face a short-term closure as operations transition to a new operator. The 59-year lease held by the Royal Gorge Company of Colorado ends Saturday night.

The outgoing company's tenure brought concept expansions and popular additions including the gondola and zip-lines, and it oversaw rebuilding after a 2013 wildfire that spared the bridge but destroyed nearly all park structures. The incoming operator, identified as CMBH, said it has been unable to access the property.

As a result, the company is uncertain when the park will open. It was also unclear whether the current operator will continue running the park until the lease expires.

topStory.headline: Federal Judge Bars Justice Department From Threatening Election Officials Over Ballots Ahead of Nov. 3 Midterms
topStory.summary:
U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson, based in California, issued an eight-page order late Friday barring the Trump administration from threatening, intimidating or coercing state and local election officials or workers. The order specifically prohibits demands that officials halt processing or segregate the ballots of any registered voter solely because the administration alleges the voter is ineligible. It remains in effect through Nov. 16, nearly two weeks after Election Day.

In her ruling, Thompson wrote that high-ranking Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security officials have engaged in a campaign to intimidate, threaten and coerce officials and employees administering the 2026 midterm election. She wrote that although the government says its actions are meant to halt unlawful voting by noncitizens, they are likely to interfere with election administration and disenfranchise lawful voters. A Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement that federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting and that enforcing the law is the department's job.

The order follows a push by the administration to make states, including California and Washington, separate out ballots it says may have been cast by noncitizens. The Justice Department sent letters to election officials in 57 of California's 58 counties, directing them to cooperate with investigations or face scrutiny themselves. An Oct. 22 letter to San Bernardino County from First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bilal Essayli attached a list of 1,133 "likely aliens," asked for Social Security numbers and driver's license or state ID data within 48 hours, and requested that vote-by-mail ballots of individuals whose citizenship could not be confirmed be segregated, not canceled. Essayli has also warned that any election official who knowingly processes a noncitizen's ballot is exposing themselves to legal jeopardy.

The ruling came the same day the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals rejected, 2-1, the Justice Department's request that California set aside disputed ballots. The administration alleges the state sent ballots to about 20,000 people who may not be citizens, while California officials say the list is highly unreliable and likely includes many citizens. The panel wrote that there is no feasible way to identify and segregate specific individuals' ballots without potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system. The majority opinion came from Judge Mark J. Bennett, appointed by President Trump, and Judge Gabriel P. Sanchez, appointed by former President Joe Biden. A district court judge had denied the request Wednesday.

The disputes carry immediate consequences as voting nears its end. Millions of Californians have already voted, and hundreds of thousands of ballots have been processed, which election officials say cannot be matched back to individual voters. The Washington case remains pending, and the Thompson order sets limits on federal pressure on election workers through the period when ballots are counted and results certified.
